To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

health providers’ narratives about intimate partner violence against Roma women in Spain are dominated by oppressive internalized stories and that they need to be challenged with resistant views of negative interpretations.

Health providers' narratives on intimate partner violence against Roma women in Spain are characterized by the prevalence of dominant and adaptive narratives, and that liberating narratives are not as salient.

the narratives of healthcare professionals in Spain about IPV against Roma women are dominated by oppressive, internalized, and negative stereotypes about Roma people and women, with few liberating narratives that challenge oppression and stereotypes.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the way in which the narratives of health professionals about IPV against Roma women are constructed and the implications that this may have for the treatment that Roma women who are victims of IPV receive in the healthcare system.
the way in which dominant narratives are used in health providers’ discourses to construct Roma women as a marginalized and stigmatized group, and to normalize IPV.
the way in which health professionals' narratives about the Roma people and IPV affect their responses to Roma women's health needs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the narratives of the health professionals in the present study were predominantly negative, with the exception of a few positive narratives that were used in a very restricted manner.
health providers’ narratives on IPV and Roma women are mainly dominated by oppressive and prejudicial narratives that reflect the negative stereotypes that exist in Spain about this ethnic group.

this study identifies how the dominant, adaptive and liberating narratives are used by health providers in Spain when talking about intimate-partner violence (IPV), and the health system response to the way that it affects Roma women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we need to be aware that the way in which health providers talk about Roma women and IPV is not neutral, and it has an important impact on the way in which these women are treated in the health system, which in turn affects their access to health care and the way in which they are treated.
health providers' narratives about Roma people in the context of IPV against Roma women are mainly negative and discriminatory.
health providers’ narratives on IPV against Roma women are shaped by dominant, adaptive, or liberating narratives.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the narratives used by health providers when talking about IPV and Roma women are not only related to their own personal experiences and perceptions but also to the social and cultural environment in which these professionals are located.
health providers' dominant narratives are the most prevalent and that they are not only related to IPV but also to the way they talk about Roma women.
the use of liberating narratives can help health professionals to be more sensitive and to better understand and respond to IPV against Roma women.
